terms.grammar: noun, second declension; with genitive or ad
evidence: Cic. Arch. 23: et perīculōrum et labōrum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Whatever spurs someone on: glory, a reward, an example; in Tacitus also of a person who urges on (incitāmentum mortis).
Something that draws one on, an invitation to act: Cicero sets an honour that is an invītāmentum ad tempus against one that is the reward of lasting merit (below).
The ox-goad, and figuratively whatever pricks one on, as in English.
Where the incentive is a prize or a payment (see reward).

phrases.latin: is autem nōn invītāmentum ad tempus, sed perpetuae virtūtis praemium
phrases.english: an honour that is no passing inducement, but the reward of lasting merit

phrases.latin: inclīnātiō senātūs incitāmentum Tiberiō fuit quō prōmptius adversārētur
phrases.english: the senate’s leaning was an incentive to Tiberius to oppose him the more readily

sources: Lewis & Short: incitamentum · Lewis & Short: invitamentum · Lewis & Short: stimulus · Lewis & Short: praemium
